habitat: Beluga whales inhabit Arctic and sub-Arctic waters, primarily in the coastal areas of Alaska, Canada, Greenland, Norway, and Russia. They are found in the Arctic Ocean and adjoining seas, including the Bering Sea, Hudson Bay, Gulf of St. Lawrence, and Sea of Okhotsk. During summer, belugas migrate into estuaries and shallow coastal waters, sometimes swimming far up rivers. In winter, they move to deeper offshore waters where ice coverage is less extensive.
diet: Belugas are opportunistic feeders with a diverse diet of fish, squid, octopus, shrimp, crabs, clams, and marine worms. They consume 2-3% of their body weight daily — roughly 25-50 kilograms of food. Using echolocation, they locate prey in murky or dark Arctic waters. They have flexible necks that can turn side to side, helping them scan the seafloor for food. Belugas lack a dorsal fin, an adaptation that allows them to swim under ice sheets.
behavior: Belugas are highly social animals, living in pods of 2-25 individuals that may aggregate into groups of hundreds during migration. They are known as the 'canaries of the sea' for their diverse vocal repertoire of clicks, whistles, squeals, and chirps — sounds used for communication and echolocation. Belugas are curious and playful, frequently approaching boats and interacting with humans. They can swim backward, a rare ability among cetaceans.
facts: Belugas are born dark gray and gradually lighten, achieving their distinctive white coloration at 5-12 years of age — a process believed to provide camouflage in icy waters. Their bulbous forehead, called a 'melon,' is a fatty organ used for echolocation that can change shape to focus sound. Belugas can dive to depths of 700 meters and hold their breath for up to 25 minutes. They can live 30-50 years in the wild.
naming: Beluga-themed names might reflect their Arctic home, white color, and musical nature. Consider names like Glacier, Pearl, Ivory, Echo, Symphony, Frost, Snow, Winter, Melody, Crystal, Aurora (after the northern lights), Nix (Latin for snow), Lumia (snow in Finnish), or Bianca (white in Italian).
